findings.matters: A target of this size applied to establishment costs is a concrete savings commitment that other councils and lenders can track against delivery.
findings.figures: 10% establishment savings, moving to 15% within three years

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Report: Community Infrastructure Levy and section 106 Policies - Enforcement Policy and Spending Policy - Overview & Scrutiny Committee - 04/11/2026
findings.headline: The draft CIL spending policy states that any overspend on a funded project is the responsibility of the infrastructure provider, not the Council.
findings.detail: The paper says contracts with infrastructure providers will indemnify the Council for misuse of funds, overspends and legal challenge. The policy also says providers must repay funding where it is misused or the project cannot proceed. The Council says it will not underwrite overspends.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council structuring grant funding for third-party infrastructure will want to compare how risk and repayment obligations are passed to providers.
findings.quote: The contract will be clear that any overspends will be the responsibility of the infrastructure provider

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Report: Community Infrastructure Levy and section 106 Policies - Enforcement Policy and Spending Policy - Overview & Scrutiny Committee - 04/11/2026
findings.headline: S106 spending rules say projects should not commence until the Council has received the money, unless the S151 Officer agrees otherwise.
findings.detail: The draft policy states that projects funded through S106 agreements, internal or external, should not start until the Council holds the money. The exception is where the S151 Officer agrees. Where the spending of monies is with a third party, the policy requires a master contract that indemnifies the Council.
findings.matters: A finance director deciding whether to advance project spend ahead of receipts will see the rule and the S151 exception written into the policy.
findings.quote: Note, that no projects (internal or external) to be funded through S106 agreements should commence

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Report: Community Infrastructure Levy and section 106 Policies - Enforcement Policy and Spending Policy - Overview & Scrutiny Committee - 04/11/2026
findings.headline: The draft policy states that CIL and S106 monies cannot be used to address existing deficits.
findings.detail: The paper's appendix says CIL and S106 can only fund newly arising demand from growth. It adds that a deficit will highlight the need for improvements in infrastructure in the first instance. The CIL spending criteria also say CIL should not be used simply to remedy an existing deficit.
findings.matters: Finance officers at councils with infrastructure backlogs need to know that developer contributions cannot be used to close them, so they must be funded from other sources.
findings.quote: CIL and S106 monies cannot be used to address existing deficits

findings.detail: The Council Housing risk records that the repairs budget was not adequate because stock condition records were lacking. The paper says the entire HRA account is going through a zero-budgeted reset, and additional budget has been approved.

findings.matters: Decent Homes compliance and a completed condition survey are the inputs a finance director needs to judge the scale of HRA capital investment ahead of 2027/28 budget setting.

findings.detail: The paper records a smaller budget pressure in the Housing Revenue Account. The HRA business case is to be reviewed as part of 2027/28 budget setting, which the council says it will use to fully re-baseline the account.

findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Sustainability risk records a General Fund pressure forecast at Q1 2026/27. The paper says works are underway on in-year mitigations and on 2027/28 budget setting to return the General Fund to a balanced position. The risk trend is shown as Decreasing.

findings.detail: The action to bring in additional capacity or backfill for officers working on LGR is still ongoing, with budget in place and joint resourcing with partner authorities. The paper also says initial priorities will be revised for "the pause on LGR".

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: LGA Corporate Peer Challenge noted limited progress on finance approach and identified need for more robust approaches to forecasting and managing financial position.
findings.detail: The LGA Corporate Peer Challenge follow-up report in November 2025 noted progress on operational improvements but identified scepticism from officers and elected members regarding robustness and effectiveness of finance and budget-setting processes. The report stated that finance is an area where progress against recommendations has been limited.
findings.matters: External peer challenge assessment of weak finance governance, combined with demonstrated forecasting failures and structural budget issues, creates a composite picture of financial management weakness material to lender assessment of council creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Not applicable
findings.quote: The approach to finance is an area in which progress against the corporate peer challenge recommendations would appear to be limited. We see a need to develop more robust, collective and transparent approaches to forecasting and managing the authority's financial position.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Budget identified as hard to interrogate due to convoluted internal recharges obscuring base position; Cabinet approved budget re-basing to increase transparency.
findings.detail: The interim finance director identified that the budget has proven hard to interrogate with convoluted internal recharges obscuring the base position. This makes it more challenging for budget holders to be held accountable or manage their budgets effectively. Cabinet approved re-basing of budgets, simplifying internal recharges to statutory required levels, and adjusting service budgets for technical accounting adjustments. New centralised processes for legal, IT and property spending are being implemented.
findings.matters: Budget opacity and inability of budget holders to control their own variances signals financial management infrastructure failure; while re-basing is welcome, the prior lack of identification is concerning to lenders.
findings.figures: £8,335k base budget approved for re-basing and simplification
findings.quote: Overall, the budget has proven hard to interrogate with convoluted internal recharges obscuring the base position. This also makes it more challenging for budget holders to be held to account or for them to manage their budgets effectively. To ensure transparency and to ensure the budget is soundly set, the budget will need correcting.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation pause has invalidated prior planning assumptions and required Council to address reserves spent in anticipation of vesting day obligations.
findings.detail: The pausing of LGR has created significant uncertainty. The Council had made decisions assuming LGR on 1 April 2028, spending reserves at higher levels to fund improvements necessary to meet Vesting Day obligations. With LGR now delayed, the Council must work with neighbouring councils to recover resources from Central Government if possible and refocus resources assuming LGR will be delayed or may not happen. The LGR budget line shows £250k allocation for 2026/27, now presumed to be repurposed.
findings.matters: The LGR pause invalidates a strategic planning assumption; reserves spent in anticipation of merger economies of scale must now be replaced through other means, adding to structural deficit pressure.
findings.figures: LGR budget £250k (2026/27) showing £236k favourable variance as budget presumed to be re-purposed
findings.quote: LGR pausing has created significant uncertainty through local government and, at the time of writing this report, there was no guidance or further information from Government as to the scope or duration of the pause, or its likely outcomes. [...] Now LGR is delayed, it will need to work with neighbouring councils to recover resources from Central Government if possible and to refocus and rebuild its own resources on the assumption that LGR, will be delayed, if it happens at all.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Without corrective action, Council would require Extraordinary Financial Support by 2028/29 to balance budget.
findings.detail: Finance modelling shows that if no action is taken, the Council would require Extraordinary Financial Support by 2028/29. The modelling demonstrates a trajectory where a recurring overspend of approximately £4.5 million continues annually. The Section 151 Officer has indicated members will not tolerate an imbalanced budgetary position and that the MTFP must be sustainable and credibly deliverable.
findings.matters: A trajectory toward requiring Extraordinary Financial Support signals the council has moved from transient pressures to structural imbalance and represents formal escalation of financial distress with external intervention risk.
findings.figures: £4.467 million recurring deficit 2026/27 onwards; cumulative savings requirement £8.5 million by 2031/32; opening reserves £23.017 million declining to nil by 2028/29 in no-action scenario
findings.quote: Finance has modelled the position to demonstrate what would happen if no action was taken. Very clearly, it evidences that by 2028/29, the Council would require Extraordinary Financial Support (EFS) to balance its budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecast overspend of £0.674 million, with HRA unallocated reserves expected to move to almost zero.
findings.detail: The HRA shows a forecast overspend of £674k. Pressures include £60k employee costs, £120k repairs and compliance, £80k specialist support and £70k IT costs. These are partially offset by £550k higher than expected rental income and service charges. The Council expects the £674k deficit to be met from HRA unallocated reserves, which are forecast to move to almost zero.
findings.matters: Depletion of HRA reserves to near-zero leaves the account with no buffer for demand fluctuations or cost pressures and suggests the HRA business plan may not be sustainable without further intervention.
findings.figures: £674k forecast overspend; £550k higher rental and service charge income; HRA reserves moving to almost zero
findings.quote: There is no forecast use of reserves at present but the £674k will be expected to come from the HRA Unallocated Reserves. Overall, reserves are likely to move to almost zero.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation pressure of £550k with probable outcome range £0 to £1.1m pending nightly lets assessment process improvements
findings.detail: The Council faces £550k pressure on temporary accommodation, with a range of probable outcomes from £0 to £1.1 million pending resolution of nightly lets assessment processes. The root cause is that individuals were not being assessed correctly, resulting in incorrect Housing Benefit calculations. However, the impact is not retrospective; correct assessment only benefits the Council from the date of reassessment forward.
findings.matters: A housing benefit assessment failure of this scale indicates operational weakness in a statutory function and creates an open-ended financial exposure with no retrospective recovery; the uncertainty range signals ongoing operational risk.
findings.figures: £550k forecast pressure; range of probable outcomes £0 to £1.1 million
findings.quote: There is a £0.55 million of Temporary Accommodation pressure retained corporately. Significant work is being undertaken in the Housing service to make improvements to the nightly lets processes, but as that is not yet completed, a range of probable outcomes from £0 to £1.1 million is assumed.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Waste and Recycling £400k overspend on tipping and recycling costs identified as reasonably foreseeable expenditure that should have been incorporated in base budget.
findings.detail: Waste and Recycling shows £400k overspend on recycling, tipping, repairs and parts costs, plus £90k overspend on fuel and hire costs and £150k unachievable kitchen and garden waste income. The Council notes this was reasonably predictable expenditure — even rolling forward prior-year costs would have identified the pressure — and should have been incorporated at a higher level.
findings.matters: Failure to budget for predictable recurring cost pressures (waste contract inflation, known waste volumes) suggests weak budget discipline and inadequate forward planning in a service where costs are inherently predictable.
findings.figures: £400k overspend on recycling, tipping, repairs and parts; £90k overspend on fuel and hire; £150k unachievable income; net Waste & Recycling overspend £456k
findings.quote: This was reasonably predictable, even rolling forward last year costs would have meant this should have been incorporated in the base budget at a higher level.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Recreation service forecasts £610k unachievable fee income, with Council noting historic pattern of optimistic income targets in leisure services.
findings.detail: Recreation service forecasts £610k unachievable fee income, primarily from classes and memberships (£470k). The Council explicitly notes a historic pattern of optimistic income targets in this area and that 2026/27 budget uplifts made the situation worse. This represents a permanent ongoing revenue pressure. Additional overspends include £290k in leisure and £180k on property costs, with many budget variances netting off.
findings.matters: A pattern of systematically optimistic income forecasts in discretionary services indicates weak demand management or unreliable budget-setting processes, creating structural pressure that cannot be grown away and must be addressed through savings.
findings.figures: £610k unachievable fee income (primarily £470k from classes and memberships); £290k leisure overspend; £180k property cost overspend; net Recreation overspend £1.052 million
findings.quote: There is £610k unachievable fee income predicted, primarily from classes and memberships income (£470k) but this appears to have been overstated and so the income target needs reviewing. [...] It is worth noting that there is a historic pattern of optimistic income targets in this area and 2026/27 budget uplifts made the situation worse.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Structural budget issues identified: approved staffing requirements and costs not fully reflected in base budget despite necessity for safe and legal service delivery.
findings.detail: Early findings indicate approved staffing requirements and associated costs were not fully reflected in the Council's base budget despite being necessary to ensure safe and legal delivery of services. Service review decisions when approved were not necessarily incorporated into the medium-term financial plan. A comprehensive review of staffing budgets is being undertaken to accurately reflect service needs and statutory obligations, with outcomes to be reported to Cabinet on 16 December 2026.
findings.matters: Staffing necessary for statutory compliance and safety not being budgeted suggests either inadequate financial planning or a pattern of unfunded service improvements — both carry risk that future budget pressures will be similarly underestimated.
findings.figures: £1.3 million projected salary overspending (£0.8 million highly certain; £0.5 million high-level estimate for health and safety posts); £500k centrally held corporate salary risk
findings.quote: However, early findings suggest that some approved staffing requirements and associated costs were not fully reflected in the Council's base budget even though significant improvements were necessary to ensure safe and legal delivery of services.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: 2025/26 outturn £2.126m overspend (£0.431m after reserves) not forecast in quarterly Cabinet reports; investigation underway into forecasting
findings.detail: The financial year end 2025/26 resulted in a significant overspend which was not forecast in quarterly reporting to Cabinet on 16 September 2025, 23 December 2025, or 18 March 2026. The Council is investigating why this happened and has opened discussions with external auditors about the conduct and focus of the 2025/26 audit. This forecasting failure prompted the review of structural budget issues now evident in quarter 1.
findings.matters: Failure to forecast a significant overspend across multiple quarterly reports raises questions about forecasting capability, financial controls, and the reliability of future projections — material to lender assessment of financial management quality and risk of further surprises.

The disclaimer will continue into future years until assurance can be built up on all areas of the accounts. This means the auditor cannot provide full assurance on opening balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion for four consecutive years severely undermines the credibility of financial statements and indicates unresolved historical control or verification issues that extend back to 2021/22.
findings.quote: This will continue unto future years until assurance can be built up on all areas of the Accounts.

findings.paper_title: Addendum: Item 4 Report: Financial Statements and External Auditors Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Trade receivables doubled while impairment coverage fell, signalling growing collection difficulty
findings.detail: Gross trade receivables increased from £1.541m to £2.846m, yet impairment allowances for bad debts fell from £926k to £699k. Net position improved only because gross receivables were higher, but the trend suggests the council is extending credit or experiencing slower collections.
findings.matters: Rising receivables and falling impairment provisions indicate either optimism about collection (unjustified) or weakening debtor quality. Both concern lenders because it signals cash timing risk.
findings.figures: Gross trade receivables: £1.541m to £2.846m; Impairment: £926k to £699k
findings.quote: Trade receivables 1,541 to 2,846 [and] Less impairment allowances for bad and doubtful debts (926) to (699)

findings.paper_title: Addendum: Item 4 Report: Financial Statements and External Auditors Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Material prior year adjustment: £1.8m government grant now deemed irrecoverable, reducing reserves retroactively
findings.detail: A £1.8m government grant receivable recognised at 31 March 2024 has been retroactively removed because it is now deemed irrecoverable from the relevant Central Government department. This required a prior period adjustment to restate 2023/24 comparatives and reduced General Fund reserves from £5.859m to £3.999m.
findings.matters: Loss of an expected £1.8m grant reduces the council's financial resilience. The retroactive adjustment indicates governance weakness in grant claim verification and suggests other receivables may carry similar collection risk.
findings.figures: Prior period adjustment: £1.8m; Impact on General Fund: from £5.859m to £3.999m
findings.quote: Management have subsequently identified that the receivable was incorrectly recognised as it was irrecoverable from the Central Government department at that date.

findings.paper_title: Addendum: Item 4 Report: Financial Statements and External Auditors Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council received £4.5m from borrowing and repaid £6.9m in 2024/25, reducing net debt while cash position deteriorated
findings.detail: Cash receipts from borrowing were £4.5m while repayments totalled £6.9m, for a net reduction in debt. This occurred while the council's cash position deteriorated to overdraft, suggesting it is borrowing less while liquidity worsens.
findings.matters: A council reducing net borrowing while cash position deteriorates suggests either squeezed PWLB access, reduced appetite for new debt, or prioritisation of repayment over operations.
findings.figures: Cash receipts from borrowing: (4,500)k; Repayments: 6,900k
findings.quote: Cash receipts from short term and long term borrowing (4,500) [and] Repayments of short term and long term borrowing 6,900

findings.paper_title: Addendum: Item 4 Report: Financial Statements and External Auditors Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Operating cash flow swung from £229k inflow in 2023/24 to £4.923m outflow in 2024/25
findings.detail: Net cash from operating activities swung from a £229k inflow in 2023/24 to a £4.923m outflow in 2024/25. This means the council's core operations—funded by taxation and service income—consumed cash rather than generated it.
findings.matters: Negative operating cash flow signals the council's services are not self-funding from revenues. This is structurally unsustainable and suggests either service delivery is overspent or income is falling.
findings.figures: Net Cash from Operating Activities: (229)k inflow to (4,923)k outflow
findings.quote: Net Cash (Inflow)/Outflow from Operating Activities (229) to (4,923)

findings.paper_title: Addendum: Item 4 Report: Financial Statements and External Auditors Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council moved from positive £722k cash to negative £627k overdraft position in one year
findings.detail: Cash and equivalents fell from £722k surplus at 31 March 2024 to -£627k at 31 March 2025, a deterioration of £1.349m. This represents a fundamental shift in the council's liquidity position and suggests it is now financing operations from overdraft or restricted credit facilities.
findings.matters: Negative cash indicates the council cannot meet obligations from reserves and must rely on borrowing or overdraft. Lenders view councils with negative cash positions as higher credit risk.
findings.figures: Cash and Cash Equivalents: £722k (2023/24) to -£627k (2024/25)
findings.quote: Cash and Cash Equivalents as at 31 March 15 (627)

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Report: Housing Improvement Programme Update - Overview & Scrutiny Committee - 02/09/2026
findings.headline: Senior management vacancies in Housing Service covered by interim staff with permanent recruitment delayed
findings.detail: Key senior positions (T4 and T3 levels) in the Housing Service structure remain vacant and are filled by interim resources. The Transition Plan commits to permanent recruitment but timing and approach are still being developed, creating ongoing staffing continuity risk during a major capital investment programme.
findings.matters: Unfilled senior positions covered by temporary staff during execution of a £125+ million capital programme indicates leadership capacity risk and potential knowledge loss or inconsistent decision-making.
findings.figures: Vacancies at T4 and T3 levels (specific count not disclosed)
findings.quote: There are vacancies that remain at a senior level (T4 and T3) that are currently covered by interim resources.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Report: Housing Improvement Programme Update - Overview & Scrutiny Committee - 02/09/2026
findings.headline: Complaints handling satisfaction at 26% with 62% dissatisfaction, indicating systemic governance issues
findings.detail: Tenant Satisfaction Measures show complaints handling as the lowest-scoring service measure at 26% satisfaction and 62% dissatisfaction. The council identifies root causes as poor complaint management, timeliness of resolution, and failure to keep tenants informed. This pattern is consistent across customer service complaints analysed in the survey.
findings.matters: Widespread complaints handling failures suggest systemic governance and oversight weaknesses that extend beyond the complaints process and may affect other council services and regulatory compliance.
findings.figures: Complaints handling satisfaction 26%; dissatisfaction 62% (both lowest across 12 measures)
findings.quote: Satisfaction with Castle Point BC's complaints handling is the lowest scoring measure (26%) and also records the highest dissatisfaction (62%).

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Report: Housing Improvement Programme Update - Overview & Scrutiny Committee - 02/09/2026
findings.headline: £125.7 million capital commitment over 30 years under new Housing Revenue Account Business Plan
findings.detail: The council has committed £125.7 million over 30 years solely to maintain homes at Decent Homes Standard, with immediate spending of £1.2 million in 2026/27 for communal areas and £1.3 million for sheltered housing. Additional commitments include £6.9 million for fire safety and £5 million for energy efficiency improvements, with all non-compliant homes to be remedial-complete by end of 2026/27.
findings.matters: This represents a material and sustained commitment to capital borrowing that must be financed through the HRA and affects the council's debt headroom and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £125.7m over 30 years (Decent Homes); £1.2m communal areas 2026/27; £1.3m sheltered housing 2026/27; £5m energy efficiency; £6.9m fire safety
findings.quote: £125.7 million over 30 years to maintain all Council homes at the Decent Homes Standard. All homes needing remedial work are expected to be compliant by the end of the 2026/7 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Report: Housing Improvement Programme Update - Overview & Scrutiny Committee - 02/09/2026
findings.headline: Asbestos compliance in council housing fell from 100% to 38% in June 2026 due to contractor scheduling issues, recovering by end-July
findings.detail: Asbestos compliance across council housing fell dramatically from 100% to 38% in June 2026 following scheduling issues between contractors. The council states asbestos is low or very low risk and managed on a risk-based approach, but the Compliance Manager had to reschedule assessments which were not completed until end of July. This represents a control failure in managing critical safety compliance.
findings.matters: A 62-percentage-point drop in health and safety compliance indicates weak contractor oversight and control of critical standards, raising questions about the council's ability to manage its capital programmes.
findings.figures: Asbestos compliance 100% → 38% (June 2026); recovered by end-July
findings.quote: In June 2026 asbestos compliance dropped from 100% to 38% due to scheduling issues between contractors.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Report: External Audit Provisional Plan 25/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Council's audit assurance recovery is behind schedule with unqualified opinion unlikely before 2027/28
findings.detail: The auditor explicitly states that the council's progress in rebuilding audit assurance from disclaimed to qualified to unqualified opinions is falling behind the expected timescale set out in the NAO's recovery guidance (LARRIG 01). An unqualified opinion is now unlikely before 2027/28, representing an extended multi-year period without full audit assurance.
findings.matters: A multi-year delay in achieving audit assurance indicates structural governance and financial reporting issues that will not be quickly resolved. This extends the period during which the council cannot credibly report its financial position to external stakeholders.
findings.figures: Expected recovery path: 2025/26 disclaimed; 2026/27 likely qualified; 2027/28 target for unqualified
findings.quote: In our view, the Council's progress falls behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01. And as set out in the 24/25 Audit Results Report, it is unlikely that audit assurances can be rebuilt to enable an unqualified opinion by 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Report: External Audit Provisional Plan 25/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Two material misstatements identified in 2024/25 audit, requiring performance materiality set at 50% of planning materiality
findings.detail: The auditors identified two material misstatements during the 2024/25 audit. In response, performance materiality for 2025/26 has been set at 50% of planning materiality (£0.4m vs £0.8m), a conservative threshold indicating the auditors' reduced confidence in the quality of the financial statements and internal controls.
findings.matters: Material misstatements that were not caught by the council's own financial controls indicate weaknesses in the finance function and the control environment; the auditor's conservative approach suggests they expect more errors.
findings.figures: Two material misstatements in 2024/25; planning materiality £0.8m; performance materiality £0.4m (50% threshold)
findings.quote: We identified two material misstatements as a result of our work.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Report: External Audit Provisional Plan 25/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Procurement and contract management weaknesses led to potential fraud against the council
findings.detail: The external auditor identified weaknesses in the council's procurement and contract management arrangements that resulted in potential fraud. This is documented as a significant weakness in governance and was also identified as a risk under the value for money criteria for economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
findings.matters: Fraud losses, even potential ones, are material financial risks. Weak procurement controls indicate systemic control environment issues that could extend to financial reporting controls.
findings.figures: Identified as weakness in 2024/25; status of remediation unknown from this plan
findings.quote: Weaknesses in procurement and contract management which led to potential fraud against the Council

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Report: External Audit Provisional Plan 25/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued formal judgment of very serious failings in consumer standards delivery
findings.detail: The council received a regulatory judgment citing very serious failings in its delivery of consumer standards for social housing. This is identified as a significant weakness in the council's value for money arrangements and constitutes a regulatory intervention.
findings.matters: Regulatory sanctions against housing delivery indicate management capability issues and potential service disruption or remediation costs; lenders assess regulatory standing as an indicator of management competence.
findings.figures: Regulator of Social Housing judgment issued; specific findings documented in audit
findings.quote: The Authority has been issued with a regulatory judgment by the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) regarding very serious failings by the Council in delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Report: External Audit Provisional Plan 25/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Council Dwellings (£151.1m balance) lacks prior-year audit assurance; stock condition survey delayed until May 2025
findings.detail: The valuation of council dwellings—the largest single asset balance at £151.1 million—had no substantive audit assurance in 2024/25 because the stock condition survey required for proper valuation was not completed. The survey was only started in May 2025, five months after the financial year-end, in response to findings by the Regulator of Social Housing. This is now designated a significant audit risk for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A £151m housing asset balance is material to the council's balance sheet and financial position. Without reliable valuation evidence, the true financial position cannot be determined.
findings.figures: £151.1 million council dwellings balance at 31 March 2025; stock survey commenced May 2025
findings.quote: A Stock Condition Survey which would impact the Council Dwellings' valuation has not yet been completed. The Council commenced this survey in May 2025 as a response to a Regulator of Social Housing's finding. Council Dwellings are valued at £151 million as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Report: External Audit Provisional Plan 25/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion expected again in 2025/26 due to uncertainty over opening balances
findings.detail: The council is likely to receive a second consecutive year of disclaimed audit opinion, meaning the auditor will have no opinion on the financial statements at all. This stems from uncertainty over the opening balances and movements in-year. The path to rebuilding assurance to an unqualified opinion is now expected to take at least until 2027/28 at the earliest.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on audited financial statements for credit assessment when the auditor disclaims an opinion. This represents a fundamental gap in financial reporting assurance.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions in both 2023/24 and 2024/25; unlikely to reach unqualified status by 2026/27
findings.quote: Due to uncertainty over opening balances and therefore movements in year, the 2025/26 statements are again likely to be disclaimed.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Report: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will create significant resource diversion from April 2028
findings.detail: Castle Point will merge to form South East Essex Council from 1 April 2028 alongside Southend-on-Sea City Council, Rochford District Council and parts of Essex County Council. The council acknowledges this requires significant work and resource, and is explicitly alert to the risk that resources diverted to the transition will impact ongoing service delivery.
findings.matters: Major structural reorganisations of local government historically increase financial risk, distract management attention from operations, and create uncertainty about future financial arrangements and borrowing capacity. The four-year transition period creates an extended period of elevated risk.
findings.figures: Transition date: 1 April 2028; forms South East Essex Council
findings.quote: There is a significant amount of work and resource required to deliver the transition, and the Council is alert to the risk that the diversion of resources required to deliver these changes impacts on the ongoing delivery of services to residents and other stakeholders

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Report: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026

findings.detail: The council utilised reserves on a one-off basis to cover the 2025/26 revenue budget overspends. While the 2026/27 budget is set to be sustainable, this represents a one-time depletion of financial resilience.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to cover overspends indicates the council is not living within its means and is consuming its financial buffer. This reduces the council's ability to absorb future shocks or unexpected costs.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Report: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Housing service investigation found poor procurement, weak contract management and inadequate resourcing
findings.detail: An independent investigation into the Housing Improvement Programme uncovered issues under the previous Service Level Agreement with South Essex Homes including poor procurement practices, poor management of contracts, inadequate resources and multiple non-integrated data management systems. While the SLA has concluded and processes have improved, it demonstrates historical management capability issues.
findings.matters: The Housing Revenue Account is a separate funding stream and is material to the council's financial position. The investigation reveals prior management failures in a major service area, suggesting oversight weaknesses and potential for similar issues elsewhere.
findings.figures: Investigation scope covered spend management, contract values and budget coding issues
findings.quote: The housing service has been poorly managed in the past, with poor procurement, poor management of contracts, inadequate resources, and multiple non-integrated data management

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Report: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Financial Planning governance assessment downgraded from Satisfactory to Partial
findings.detail: The council's core financial planning, reporting and budgetary control function fell to 'Partial' from 'Satisfactory' in 2024/25. The statement notes that a recovery plan will be produced by end of July 2026 to address prior year adjustments and mitigate projected overspends, and that root cause analysis will be conducted.
findings.matters: This is the council's primary financial control mechanism. Downgrading it to 'Partial' (meaning some requirements met but less than 50%) indicates fundamental weaknesses in budgetary stewardship and control infrastructure.
findings.figures: Assessment fell from Satisfactory (2024/25) to Partial (2025/26)
findings.quote: Overall, Financial Planning, Reporting and Budgetary Control, including Value for Money is assessed as Partial, falling from the Satisfactory position reported in 2024/25

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Report: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: External auditors issued disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 accounts and made a Statutory Recommendation
findings.detail: EY could not provide an opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, with assurance being rebuilt. The auditors formally recommended that the council consolidate all recommendations from regulatory bodies and audit reports into a single action plan with quarterly reporting to council and Audit & Governance Committee, to be completed by 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion is a serious red flag indicating material control failures or uncertainties that prevent auditors from certifying the accounts. Combined with the Statutory Recommendation, it signals structural governance weaknesses requiring sustained remediation.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit; Statutory Recommendation issued 25 March 2026
findings.quote: resulted in a 'disclaimed' opinion on the financial statements as the assurance over the financial statements is being rebuilt. At the conclusion of the 2024/25 audit EY issued a formal letter on 25 March 2026 to the Chief Executive confirming that a Statutory Recommendation was being made

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Report: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 - Audit & Governance Committee - 21/07/2026
findings.headline: Revenue budget overspent significantly, with forecasting worse than expected
findings.detail: The council ended 2025/26 with overspends on both General Fund and Housing Revenue Account revenue budgets. Quarterly forecasts to Cabinet understated the eventual overspends, and more service areas overspent than predicted. The council acknowledges its forecasting arrangements need fundamental improvement to prevent repeat in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Budget forecasting is a core control. Inability to predict or manage in-year spending accurately signals weak financial discipline and limits the council's ability to manage cash and meet commitments.
findings.figures: General Fund and HRA both overspent; capital budgets underspent
findings.quote: the eventual overspends were higher than expected and more service areas ended in an overspend position than expected. This has demonstrated that the arrangements in place to adequately forecast the Council's financial position to the required high level of accuracy need to be improved

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to decline 36% over three years, from £1.75m to £1.12m
findings.detail: The council's investment income—earned from holding surplus cash—is forecast to drop sharply from £1,751k in 2024/25 to £1,121k in 2026/27 (2027/28 £1,081k), only rising modestly thereafter. This reflects both lower interest rates and potentially lower cash balances available to invest as capital spending consumes reserves.

findings.detail: The £36.5m borrowed in March 2012 for HRA self-financing is structured to mature at various points from 2025/26 through 2035/36. The council will need to refinance portions as they fall due. The strategy notes that interest rates are expected to decline from 3.75% to 3.25% by end-2026, which would be favorable for refinancing.

findings.headline: General Fund has annual funding gaps that must be closed, reflecting structural budget pressures
findings.detail: The strategy document references that the General Fund has 'annual funding gaps to be closed' and the HRA faces 'challenges such as the lasting impact of changes in central government policies', but provides no detail on size or solution. This signals underlying budget imbalance that the council is managing but not fully transparent about.
findings.matters: Undetailed funding gaps suggest the council is facing structural budget pressures that may require service reductions, further reserves drawdown, or revenue raising—all relevant to creditworthiness
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document

findings.paper_title: Item 4 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2029/30- Special Council - 11/02/2026
findings.headline: Council Tax increase constrained at 2.98%, just below 3% referendum threshold
findings.detail: Council Tax band D increase is set at exactly 2.98%, described as 'the lowest increase for any of the organisations which charge Council Tax in the Borough'. The council notes that a 3% increase or more than £5 increase would trigger a referendum. The budget appears to have been optimised to stay just below the threshold.
findings.matters: The council has limited room to raise additional income from Council Tax without holding a referendum. This constrains flexibility if savings don't land or costs rise.
findings.figures: 2.98% increase; 3% threshold for referendum trigger
findings.quote: It is proposed that the Council Tax increase is 2.98% for 2026/27. This is the lowest increase for any of the organisations which charge Council Tax in the Borough.

findings.headline: General Reserve forecast to remain only marginally above minimum required level
findings.detail: The minimum recommended General Reserve level is £3.1m. Section 5.4 states 'The level of the General Reserve planned for the end of the 2026/27 financial year, and for all future years, exceeds the minimum recommended level of £3.1m.' The phrasing 'exceeds' suggests marginal headroom, not substantial buffer. Table 6.1 (not provided in full) would show exact balances.
findings.matters: A council holding reserves only slightly above minimum has limited capacity to absorb unbudgeted cost pressures or income shocks. This tightness is consistent with using reserves for LGR costs and relying on savings delivery.

findings.quote: The level of the General Reserve planned for the end of the 2026/27 financial year, and for all future years, exceeds the minimum recommended level of £3.1m.

findings.headline: Draft budgets for 2027/28–2029/30 are balanced on current assumptions but flagged as provisional
findings.detail: The MTFS achieves the unusual position of presenting balanced budgets across all four years (section 5.3, 5.5). However, the council explicitly states 'based on the current assumptions' and 'with one-off use of the General Reserve for LGR in 2027/28'. The commentary notes 'Naturally this position may change as future assumptions are either proved or disproved.'
findings.matters: A four-year balanced forecast is uncommon and often indicates conservative or assumed savings not yet identified. The council depends on assumptions holding and savings being delivered via its transformation board.
findings.figures: Balanced budgets forecast for all years 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.quote: The draft budgets for 2027/28, 2028/29 and 2029/30 are also balanced based on the current assumptions (and with one-off use of the General Reserve for LGR in 2027/28).

findings.paper_title: Item 4 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2029/30- Special Council - 11/02/2026
findings.headline: Budget contingent on final Local Government Finance Settlement not yet received

The report states: 'At time of writing this report, there are two areas of information outstanding. The first of these is the Final Local Government Finance Settlement for 2026/27.' The council commits to publishing an addendum if material differences emerge between draft and final settlement.
findings.matters: The three-year settlement was supposed to provide stability, but the council has not yet received the final settlement for the lead year of the budget. Material adverse changes would require budget reforecasting.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2029/30- Special Council - 11/02/2026
findings.headline: £21m housing investment to reduce temporary accommodation costs is a new, unproven initiative
findings.detail: The council is budgeting £21m to bring forward four sites across the borough to deliver new housing schemes for temporary accommodation. The strategy assumes this will 'reduce reliance on bed and breakfasts and deliver long term savings' and 'reduce Temporary Accommodation costs to the Council'. No baseline cost for current temporary accommodation or savings forecast is stated in the report.
findings.matters: This is a large capital commitment (44% of the four-year £47.8m programme) justified by predicted but unquantified revenue savings. If the four sites take longer to deliver than planned, or if temporary accommodation demand remains high, the council will have borrowed capital without the expected revenue benefit.
findings.figures: £21m across four sites; 'largest capital programme this Council has ever seen at £47.8m over the next four years'
findings.quote: The Council has also budgeted £21m to bring forward four sites across the Borough to deliver new housing schemes which will increase the provision of temporary accommodation for people and families in the Borough experiencing homelessness. The s151 officer has also 'considered a further amount of £250,000 when determining the recommended minimum level for the General Reserve' — effectively reserving £250,000 as additional LGR contingency on top of the £3.1m minimum.
findings.matters: LGR is a known but unquantified cost. The council is drawing reserves to manage it, which reduces financial flexibility. Total provision (£250k + £500k + £250k contingency = £1m) against an unknown final cost signals planning but also uncertainty.
findings.figures: £250,000 in 2026/27; £500,000 in 2027/28; further £250,000 contingency included in minimum reserve calculation
findings.quote: The Council has made budget provision of £250,000 in 2026/27 and £500,000 in 2027/28 for LGR, whilst the section 151 officer has considered a further amount of £250,000 when determining the recommended minimum level for the General Reserve.

news_drafts.headline: Castle Point's risk register records a "major overspend" on temporary accommodation, with nightly lets being cut
news_drafts.lead:
Castle Point Council's corporate risk register, presented to its Audit & Governance Committee on 3 November 2026, records a review of temporary accommodation needs that is "revealing major overspend on TA". The entry sits under the council's Homelessness risk, which has a current risk score of 9 and a target risk date of 31 March 2027. The risk owner notes the risk remains unchanged.

The register says the budget overspend "is being addressed by reducing numbers in nighty lets", a phrase quoted as it appears in the paper. A further review of progress is planned for the end of quarter 2. The same entry lists other controls: a review of the council's private sector leasing approach, procurement, rent setting and leases. The register gives no figure for the size of the overspend.

A separate paper, the committee's monitoring report on the governance arrangements set out in the council's Annual Governance Statement, lists an action to produce a recovery plan. The plan is to address any prior year adjustments deemed necessary and to mitigate projected overspends through in-year adjustments, with an end date of July 2026. The action plan also refers to "unsighted overspends in 2026/27" and to the need for stronger challenge of budget holders. The papers do not say which services those overspends are in.

news_drafts.headline: Castle Point forecasts £4.5m General Fund overspend for 2026/27 after £2.1m gap in 2025/26
news_drafts.lead:
Castle Point Council is forecasting a £4.5m overspend on its day-to-day General Fund budget for 2026/27, Cabinet was told on 14 October, with probable outcomes between £4m and £5m. The figure rests on one quarter's data and a line-by-line budget review is continuing. The main pressures are £1.3m on salaries, £0.8m of income that will not be achieved, £0.9m of legal costs for planning appeals and the Castle Point Plan, and £0.55m on temporary accommodation.

The 2025/26 outturn (the actual figures once the year had ended) showed a General Fund overspend of £2.126m before use of reserves. Drawing on money set aside for housing and another earmarked fund cut it to £0.431m, which the council's general reserve absorbs. That reserve falls to £4.471m, which is £1.371m above its approved minimum of £3.1m. Housing carried the largest pressure: £1.225m on temporary accommodation and £340k on mainly interim staff. In the separate housing revenue account, funded by rents, the overspend was £0.891m, with £526k from staffing. For 2026/27 that account is forecast to overspend by £674k, to come from its unallocated reserves, which would fall to almost zero.

The papers say the 2025/26 overspend was not forecast in quarterly reports to Cabinet on 16 September 2025, 23 December 2025 or 18 March 2026. An investigation is under way, and the council is talking to its external auditors about the 2025/26 audit. The interim chief finance officer's review found structural issues in the budget that imply a similar trajectory for 2026/27 and later years unless corrective action is taken. The papers say £400k of waste and recycling overspend on tipping and recycling costs was "reasonably predictable".

news_drafts.headline: Castle Point admits unquantified financial risk in housing enforcement policy
news_drafts.lead: Castle Point Council has adopted a housing enforcement policy that allows it to carry out remedial works on properties where landlords have breached safety standards, then recharged the costs to the responsible party. However, the council's own papers acknowledge "an unknown unquantified risk from the individuals not being able to pay," creating potential bad debts that could fall back on the council. The policy was approved without an estimate of this exposure, and the council asserts the policy requires no new budget provision, despite the admitted liability risk. The three-year policy covers 2026 to 2029.
